entry.title: SAP BAIP ABAP environment 正式落地中国：迈向 Clean Core 与云端创新的新路径
entry.content:
SAP BAIP, ABAP environment 现已在中国正式上线，为客户和合作伙伴在 SAP Business AI Platform (SAP BAIP) 上构建面向云端的 ABAP 应用与扩展提供了新的途径。

ABAP 开发在中国迎来新里程碑

2026 年 10 月 15 日，SAP BAIP, ABAP environment 在中国正式发布，标志着 SAP 在本地市场扩展云端开发能力的重要里程碑。

ABAP 长期以来是 SAP 业务应用开发与扩展的核心。随着企业推进 SAP 系统的现代化改造，他们需要在采用云端开发实践的同时，保留现有的 ABAP 专业积累与既有投资。

SAP BAIP, ABAP environment 通过提供云优化的 ABAP 平台来满足这一需求，支持应用与扩展程序的开发和运行。它使客户能够复用 ABAP 技能与资产、构建 side-by-side 扩展，并将自定义代码与数字核心解耦——助力 Clean Core 方法落地，加快创新迭代节奏。

随着该服务在中国上线，上述能力现已通过本地 SAP BAIP 正式对外提供。

现已提供哪些内容？

该服务基于 BTPEA 商业模式提供，SKU 为 8016044（面向客户的 BTPEA SKU），包含以下服务计划：

服务名称服务计划名称
ABAP environmentFree
ABAP environmenthana_compute_unit
ABAP environmentabap_compute_unit
ABAP environmentstandard
ABAP SolutionStandard
Landscape PortalStandard
Web access for ABAPWeb Access for ABAP Environment

该服务在以下两个数据中心可用：

  • 中国（华北3）— cn20
  • 中国（上海）— cn40

客户和合作伙伴可通过 SAP Discovery Center 查看可用地区与服务计划：

  • 中国（华北3）— ABAP environment
  • 中国（上海）— ABAP environment

中国 BTPEA 价格表中列出了 SAP BAIP, ABAP environment 的可计费计划，包括：

  • Free
  • 16 GB Runtime and 64 GB Persistence
  • Standard

SAP 社区已发布博客文章 SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment on Alibaba Cloud，宣布 Steampunk 在多云厂商的支持上迈出了新的一步。此次新增区域是对现有 SAP Cloud Infrastructure、AWS、Microsoft Azure 和 Google Cloud 区域的补充。

为何重要

支持 Clean Core 与云端转型

SAP BAIP, ABAP environment 的一大核心优势在于支持 side-by-side 扩展。客户可以在独立于 SAP S/4HANA 核心的环境中构建自定义应用与扩展，有效降低自定义代码与核心业务流程之间的耦合度。

这种方式有助于构建更具升级稳定性的架构，使组织能够更灵活地独立演进其扩展程序，尤其适合正在推进 SAP S/4HANA 现代化与 Clean Core 战略的企业。

延续现有 ABAP 专业积累

云端转型并不意味着放弃既有的开发专业能力。通过提供基于云的 ABAP 开发与运行环境，SAP 帮助客户和合作伙伴在采用 ABAP Cloud 开发模型的同时，持续发挥其 ABAP 专业知识的价值。

这为延伸现有能力、开发新业务功能、以及基于云端基础扩展 SAP 解决方案打开了新的空间。

扩展本地 SAP BAIP 创新渠道

在中国（华北3）和中国（上海）同步上线，进一步扩展了中国客户和合作伙伴在 SAP BAIP 上的选择空间。

这也强化了支持企业应用现代化、合作伙伴创新以及 SAP 核心业务解决方案演进的本地开发能力组合。

ABAP 云端开发在中国正式迈入新阶段。

entry.title: Bringing SAP BAIP, ABAP Environment to China: Expanding the Path to Clean Core and Cloud Innovation
entry.content:
SAP BAIP, ABAP Environment is now available in China, giving customers and partners a new way to build cloud-ready ABAP applications and extensions on SAP Business AI Platform.

A New Milestone for ABAP Development in China

On October 15, 2026, SAP BAIP, ABAP environment was released in China, marking an important milestone in expanding SAP's cloud development capabilities for the local market.

ABAP has long been central to the development and extension of SAP business applications. As enterprises modernize their SAP landscapes, they need ways to preserve their ABAP expertise and existing investments while adopting cloud-ready development practices.

SAP BAIP, ABAP environment addresses this need by providing a cloud-optimized ABAP platform for developing and running applications and extensions. It enables customers to reuse ABAP skills and assets, build side-by-side extensions, and decouple custom code from the digital core—supporting a Clean Core approach and more flexible innovation cycles.

With its availability in China, these capabilities can now be accessed through the local SAP BAIP commercial offering.

What Is Now Available?

The service is offered under the BTPEA commercial model, under SKU 8016044 (the customer-facing BTPEA SKU), with the following service plans:

Service: Display NameService Plan: Display Name
ABAP environmentFree
ABAP environmenthana_compute_unit
ABAP environmentabap_compute_unit
ABAP environmentstandard
ABAP SolutionStandard
Landscape PortalStandard
Web access for ABAPWeb Access for ABAP Environment

The service is available in two data centers:

  • China (North 3) — cn20
  • China (Shanghai) — cn40

Customers and partners can explore the available regions and service plans through SAP Discovery Center:

  • China (North 3) — ABAP Environment
  • China (Shanghai) — ABAP Environment

The China BTPEA price list also lists the available billable plans for SAP BAIP, ABAP environment, including:

  • Free
  • 16 GB Runtime and 64 GB Persistence
  • Standard

A blog post, SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment on Alibaba Cloud, has been published announcing that Steampunk has reached the next milestone in its multi‑hyperscaler availability for our customers, partners, and SAP products using Steampunk. This new offering complements the existing regions on SAP Cloud Infrastructure, AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud.

Why This Matters

Supporting Clean Core and Cloud Transformation

A key benefit of SAP BAIP, ABAP environment is its support for side-by-side extensibility. Customers can build custom applications and extensions separately from their SAP S/4HANA core, helping reduce coupling between custom code and core business processes.

This approach supports a more upgrade-stable architecture and gives organizations greater flexibility to evolve their extensions independently. It is particularly relevant for enterprises pursuing SAP S/4HANA modernization and Clean Core initiatives.

Building on Existing ABAP Expertise

Cloud transformation does not mean leaving existing development expertise behind. By providing a cloud-based ABAP development and runtime environment, SAP helps customers and partners continue to leverage their ABAP knowledge while adopting the ABAP Cloud development model.

This creates opportunities to modernize custom applications, develop new business capabilities, and extend SAP solutions using familiar skills and a cloud-ready foundation.

Expanding Local Access to SAP BAIP Innovation

Making the service available in both China (North 3) and China (Shanghai) expands the options available to customers and partners building on SAP BAIP in China.

It also strengthens the local portfolio of development capabilities that support enterprise application modernization, partner innovation, and the evolution of SAP-centric business solutions.

A new chapter for cloud-ready ABAP development in China has begun.

entry.title: Bringing SAP BAIP, Kyma Runtime to China: Expanding Cloud-Native Development Capabilities
entry.content:
SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime is now available in China, extending the local SAP BAIP portfolio with a managed Kubernetes-based runtime for cloud-native applications, microservices, and SAP extensions.

Bringing Cloud-Native Innovation Closer to Chinese Customers

Modern enterprises increasingly need to extend business applications, connect systems, and deliver new digital capabilities without introducing unnecessary complexity into their core landscapes.

SAP BAIP in China already offers Cloud Foundry runtime as a mature PaaS option for deploying applications using buildpack-based workflows. Kyma runtime addresses a different set of needs. Built on the open-source Kyma project and Kubernetes, it gives development teams direct access to container-based workloads, serverless functions, and the broader Kubernetes ecosystem—without restriction on programming language or framework. Any workload that can be containerized can run on Kyma runtime.

On June 2, 2026, SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime became available in China (North 3), followed by China (Shanghai) on July 10, 2026—making this managed cloud-native application runtime available through the local BTPEA commercial offering across both regions.

What Is Now Available?

SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime is offered under the BTPEA commercial model, under SKU 8016044 (the customer-facing BTPEA SKU), with the following service plans:

Service: Display NameService Plan: Display NameAvailable Data Center
Kyma RuntimeKyma Runtime Alibaba CloudChina (Shanghai) — cn40
Kyma RuntimeKyma Runtime AzureChina (North 3) — cn20

Customers and partners can explore the service and its regional availability through SAP Discovery Center:

  • China (North 3) — Kyma Runtime
  • China (Shanghai) — Kyma Runtime

The China BTPEA price list lists the Standard plan as a billable plan for SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime.

Why This Matters

A Managed, Flexible Foundation for Cloud-Native Applications

Running Kubernetes in-house requires ongoing investment in cluster management, upgrades, security patching, and infrastructure operations. SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime removes that burden: SAP manages the underlying platform, while customers retain full control over their applications and workloads. Development teams can focus on building business capabilities instead of maintaining infrastructure.

Compared to Cloud Foundry runtime, Kyma offers a meaningfully different development model. Cloud Foundry abstracts the runtime through buildpacks, which works well for deploying Java or Node.js applications quickly but limits what you can run and how. Kyma places no such constraints: any containerized workload runs on Kyma regardless of language or framework, and teams have direct access to Kubernetes-native tooling—Helm for packaging, custom resource definitions, fine-grained resource configuration, and the broader CNCF ecosystem. For teams building modern cloud-native applications or needing precise control over their workloads, this flexibility is a significant advantage.

The two runtimes are complementary. Cloud Foundry remains a solid choice for buildpack-based application deployment; Kyma is the better fit when container-native flexibility, polyglot development, or Kubernetes ecosystem tooling is a requirement.

Extending SAP Applications with Event-Driven Integration

Kyma runtime includes a built-in Eventing component that allows applications to subscribe directly to business events from SAP S/4HANA and other SAP systems—so an extension can react to a sales order creation, a goods movement, or a master data change in real time, without polling or point-to-point connections. Having this capability integrated into the runtime means teams can start building event-driven extensions without separately provisioning and configuring a messaging service.

Combined with serverless functions and a built-in API Gateway, this makes it practical to build lightweight, loosely coupled extensions that sit alongside the SAP core rather than inside it. Custom logic evolves independently, upgrade cycles are decoupled, and the core system remains stable.

For scenarios that go beyond SAP-to-SAP integration—connecting third-party systems, orchestrating multi-step workflows, or building net-new business applications—Kyma provides the same Kubernetes-based foundation with the flexibility to incorporate any service or technology the use case requires.

Expanding the Local SAP BAIP Development Portfolio

With Kyma runtime available in China (North 3) and China (Shanghai), customers gain an additional runtime option within the local SAP BAIP portfolio.

This is particularly relevant for teams building containerized applications, API-based integrations, event-driven extensions, and microservices that complement SAP business solutions.

The availability of Kyma runtime broadens the technology choices available to the China ecosystem and provides another foundation for cloud-native application development.

entry.title: Part 2 of 2 – Securing AI-Powered SAP Apps on SAP BTP: Single Sign-On and Role-Based Access with XSU
entry.content:
Overview

Part 1 of this series described how SAP S/4HANA data can be made available to AI clients through an MCP server running on SAP BTP. Once such data is exposed through a user interface, the application must meet the same security standards as any other access to SAP systems.

This article describes how a UI application on SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry runtime, authenticates users and enforces authorizations using two standard platform components:

  • Application router – the single entry point that handles user login and request forwarding.
  • SAP Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA) – the service that issues tokens and manages scopes, role templates and role collections.

The approach addresses three requirements:

  • Authentication: only users with a valid corporate identity can access the application.
  • Authorization: each user can access only the functions assigned to them.
  • Enforcement: authorization decisions are made on the server and cannot be bypassed in the browser.

Solution components

Component Responsibility

Identity provider (for example, SAP Cloud Identity Services connected to the corporate directory)Authenticates the user through corporate single sign-on.
XSUAAIssues a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) containing the user's scopes, based on the assigned role collections.
Application routerActs as the single public entry point. Redirects unauthenticated users to the login, maintains the user session and forwards requests to the application together with the token.
UI applicationValidates the token on every request and grants access only to the functions permitted by its scopes.

Users always access the application through the application router, and the application validates the token independently. This provides two separate layers of control.

Authentication flow

The following steps describe the first access of a user to the application:

  1. The browser requests the application through the application router. No session exists yet.
  2. The application router redirects the request to XSUAA, which delegates authentication to the configured identity provider.
  3. The user authenticates with the corporate login, typically through single sign-on.
  4. The identity provider confirms the user's identity to XSUAA. XSUAA determines the user's role collections and issues a JWT containing the corresponding scopes.
  5. The application router stores the token in its server-side session and returns the requested page. The browser receives only a session cookie.
  6. For each subsequent request, the application router attaches the token and forwards the request to the application.
  7. The application validates the token (signature, expiry and audience) and evaluates the scopes before processing the request.

 

Figure 1: Authentication flow. The highlighted arrows show where the token is transferred; it is exchanged only between server-side components.

When the session expires, the application router repeats the flow from step 2.

Authorization model

XSUAA separates the definition of permissions from their assignment through three levels:

Level Purpose Maintained by

ScopeA single permission that the application checksDeveloper, in xs-security.json
Role templateGroups one or more scopes into a functional roleDeveloper, in xs-security.json
Role collectionBundles roles for assignment to users or user groupsAdministrator, in the SAP BTP cockpit

The complete xs-security.json is shown in step 1 of the configuration below.

With this model, access is managed entirely in the SAP BTP cockpit. Granting or revoking access requires no code change and no redeployment. Assigning role collections to user groups from the identity provider, rather than to individual users, keeps access aligned with organizational changes automatically.

Configuration steps

The following examples use generic names (my-xsuaa, my-approuter, my-ui-app) and placeholders in angle brackets. Replace them with the values of your own subaccount.

Step 1: Define the security descriptor (xs-security.json)

{
  "xsappname": "my-ui-app",
  "tenant-mode": "dedicated",
  "scopes": [
    { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Display", "description": "Use the application" },
    { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Monitor", "description": "Use the monitoring functions" }
  ],
  "role-templates": [
    { "name": "Viewer",         "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Display"] },
    { "name": "MonitoringUser", "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Display", "$XSAPPNAME.Monitor"] }
  ],
  "role-collections": [
    { "name": "App Viewers",      "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Viewer"] },
    { "name": "Monitoring Users", "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.MonitoringUser"] }
  ],
  "oauth2-configuration": {
    "redirect-uris": ["https://<approuter-host>.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/**"]
  }
}

Create the XSUAA service instance from this file. Later changes are applied to the same instance with update-service:

cf create-service xsuaa application my-xsuaa -c xs-security.json
cf update-service my-xsuaa -c xs-security.json

Step 2: Configure the application router

The application router is a small Node.js application based on the @SAP/approuter package. It needs three files.

package.json:

{
  "name": "my-approuter",
  "dependencies": { "@sap/approuter": "^20" },
  "scripts": { "start": "node node_modules/@sap/approuter/approuter.js" }
}

xs-app.json – every route requires an XSUAA login, and requests are forwarded to the UI application:

{
  "welcomeFile": "/",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "logout": { "logoutEndpoint": "/logout" },
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/(.*)$",
      "target": "/$1",
      "destination": "ui-app",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    }
  ]
}

manifest.yml – the destination ui-app points to the UI application, and forwardAuthToken passes the user's token on:

applications:
  - name: my-approuter
    memory: 256M
    services:
      - my-xsuaa
    env:
      destinations: >
        [ { "name": "ui-app",
            "url": "https://<ui-app-host>.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com",
            "forwardAuthToken": true } ]

Set csrfProtection according to your application. If the UI application implements its own CSRF protection, the router's protection can be switched off for its routes, as shown above.

Step 3: Bind XSUAA to the UI application

The UI application needs the same XSUAA instance to validate the tokens it receives. Add it to the application's manifest.yml:

applications:
  - name: my-ui-app
    services:
      - my-xsuaa

Deploy both applications:

cf push my-ui-app
cf push my-approuter

Step 4: Configure trust and assign roles

In the SAP BTP cockpit, open Security → Trust Configuration and establish trust with your identity provider. Then assign the role collections under Security → Role Collections, preferably to user groups. With the SAP BTP command line interface, the assignment can also be scripted:

btp assign security/role-collection "Monitoring Users" --to-user <user@example.com>

Server-side authorization checks

The application router ensures that only authenticated users reach the application. Fine-grained authorization is performed by the application itself, on the server, for every request:

  1. Validate the forwarded token and reject requests with a missing, expired or foreign token.
  2. Read the scopes from the token.
  3. Expose only the functions and data permitted by those scopes, both in the user interface and in the server's API responses.

Because these checks run on the server, they cannot be circumvented by modifying the page or by calling the application's API directly.

For Node.js applications, SAP provides the @SAP/xssec and @SAP/xsenv packages for token validation. A minimal example with Express:

const express = require("express");
const xsenv = require("@sap/xsenv");
const { XsuaaService, createSecurityContext } = require("@sap/xssec");

const xsuaa = new XsuaaService(xsenv.getServices({ xsuaa: { tag: "xsuaa" } }).xsuaa);
const app = express();

// 1. Validate the token on every request
app.use(async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    req.authInfo = await createSecurityContext(xsuaa, { req });
    next();
  } catch (e) {
    res.status(401).json({ error: "Not authenticated" });
  }
});

// 2. Require a scope for a protected function
const requireScope = (scope) => (req, res, next) =>
  req.authInfo.checkLocalScope(scope) ? next() : res.status(403).json({ error: "Not authorized" });

app.get("/api/monitoring", requireScope("Monitor"), (req, res) => {
  res.json({ status: "ok" });   // only reached with the Monitor scope
});

app.listen(process.env.PORT || 8080);

For Java applications, the SAP Cloud Security Services Integration Library (java-security) offers the same functions.

Backend connectivity

User authentication protects access to the application. Communication between the application and SAP S/4HANA is a separate, technical connection through an SAP BTP destination and the SAP Cloud Connector, using a technical user. As a result, SAP S/4HANA authorizes the technical user rather than the individual end user.

This is suitable for a proof of concept. For productive use, principal propagation should be considered, so that the end user's own SAP authorizations are also applied in the backend system.

Handling session expiry in the UI

When the application router session expires, background requests (for example fetch calls) receive a login redirect or an HTTP 401 instead of data. A reload of the page lets the application router restart the authentication flow:

async function callApi(url, options) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { credentials: "include", ...options });
  const isJson = (res.headers.get("content-type") || "").includes("application/json");
  if (res.status === 401 || !isJson) {
    window.location.reload();        // the application router redirects to the login
    return null;
  }
  return res.json();
}

Key considerations

Topic Consideration

Role changesScopes are written into the token at login. After a role collection is assigned or removed, the user must log in again for the change to take effect.
Session expiryBackground requests cannot complete an interactive login. When a session expires, the application should reload the page so that the application router can restart the authentication flow.
Service updatesUpdates to the XSUAA instance must be applied with the intended xs-security.json. Verify the resulting roles in the SAP BTP cockpit after each update.
Client-side restrictionsHiding functions in the user interface does not replace server-side authorization checks.
CredentialsTechnical credentials, such as API keys, should be provided through service bindings rather than environment variables or source code.

Summary

The application router and XSUAA provide a UI application on SAP BTP with the same authentication and authorization model as any other SAP BTP application:

  • A single entry point with corporate single sign-on.
  • Permissions carried in a signed token, defined by developers and assigned by administrators.
  • Authorization decisions enforced on the server.

An application that exposes SAP data through AI therefore requires no dedicated security model; it integrates into the standard security concept of SAP BTP. Principal propagation is the logical next step to extend user-specific authorizations to the SAP backend.

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 3: Second Content Agent and target in Central
entry.content:
Part 3 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 2 we set up Dev, so a parcel can now be packed and dropped at the source node. In this part we build the receiving end in Central: a second Content Agent that unpacks the parcel, the connection CTMS uses to reach it, and the connection it uses to write into the target Integration Suite.

 

Before you start

The target Integration Suite runs in Central, with the Cloud Integration capability activated (the same rule as in Dev).

Step 1: Process Integration Runtime instance and key

Same as in Dev: an instance of SAP Process Integration Runtime, plan api, with the roles WorkspacePackagesRead, WorkspacePackagesEdit and WorkspacePackagesTransport, and a service key. This time it gives the unpacker access to the target workspace.

Step 2: The second Content Agent

  • Create an instance of Content Agent service with the application plan and the role Import. This is the unpacker.
  • Create a service key. You need its url and, from the uaa section, clientid, clientsecret and url.

Step 3: CloudIntegration destination in Central

The unpacker writes into Integration Suite through a destination named CloudIntegration, filled exactly like the Dev one in Part 2, but from the key of step 1. You can also let the Content Agent UI create it for you when you activate the Cloud Integration content type (see "What tripped me up" first).

Step 4: The transport destination CTMS uses

CTMS needs to know where to deliver the parcel. In Central, create a destination for that. Its name is free; I used CAS_on_target.

FieldValue
URLurl from the Content Agent key (step 2)
AuthenticationOAuth2ClientCredentials
Client ID / secretclientid / clientsecret from the uaa section
Token Service URLurl from the uaa section + /oauth/token

Step 5: Finish the target node

Open CTMS, edit the target node from Part 1 and pick CAS_on_target as its destination. The content type stays Multi-Target Application.

 

The target node with its content type and destination.

A green Check Connection on CAS_on_target only proves the address is reachable (Part 2 explains why). The real test is the first transport in Part 4.

What tripped me up in my setup

  • Three identical runtime instances. Central had three Process Integration Runtime instances with the same name, each in a different Cloud Foundry space, left over from earlier attempts. Before copying a key I had to check which space the target Cloud Integration actually runs in, and use the instance from that space. Clear names would have saved me this.
  • Activating the content type failed because the destination already existed. Activating the Cloud Integration content type in the Content Agent UI creates a CloudIntegration destination for you. I had already created one by hand, so the activation did not go through. It also asks for a Cloud Foundry passcode, and I first suspected the login URL and changed it to the Cloud Foundry API endpoint, which changed nothing. The fix was simple: I edited my existing CloudIntegration destination, added the client secret, and the activation went through. Either create the destination by hand or let the Content Agent UI do it, not both.

Roles for this part

Instance roles only: the three Workspace roles on the runtime instance and Import on the Content Agent instance. The user roles come in Part 4, and Part 7 lists them all.

What comes next

Both ends are now connected. In Part 4 we switch on Transport in Integration Suite, send the first package and import it in CTMS, including the role that kept the Transport option greyed out for me.

entry.title: Calling On-Premise Systems from Go on SAP BTP: Bindings, Tunnels and Destinations
entry.content:
The problem

While building a small Go service on SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry runtime, that had to reach two things behind an SAP Cloud Connector: an SFTP server and an OData v2 service. Before any business logic, there were three small problems to solve:

  1. Where are my credentials? On Cloud Foundry they are in VCAP_SERVICES. On SAP BTP, Kyma runtime they are files in the pod.
  2. How do I get a TCP connection through the Connectivity service? Its SOCKS5 proxy uses a login method specific to SAP.
  3. How do I turn a Destination service entry into a client I can call? The destination describes the target, but you still have to apply it yourself.

Below is how each one was solved. I'm assuming you already know how to create and bind the Destination, Connectivity and Authorization and Trust Management (XSUAA) service instances and map a virtual host in Cloud Connector.

1. Reading bindings without caring where you run

The code that reads credentials shouldn't change between Cloud Foundry and Kyma. I put both behind one small interface, with a detector that picks the right one at startup:

prov, err := auto.NewProvider()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

cb, err := binding.Connectivity(prov, "") // proxy host and ports, client id/secret
db, err := binding.Destination(prov, "")  // Destination service URI and credentials

An empty name takes the first binding of that type; pass an instance name if you have several. Detection checks VCAP_SERVICES first, then SERVICE_BINDING_ROOT, then whether a /bindings directory exists.

2. A tunnel through the Connectivity service

The Connectivity service offers a SOCKS5 proxy. Instead of the usual username/password, it expects an SAP-specific authentication method (0x80) in which you send a JWT from XSUAA. The standard library and golang.org/x/net/proxy don't implement it, so I wrote it.

You give the dialer a token source (client-credentials tokens, cached until shortly before they expire) and the proxy details from the binding:

connSrc := xsuaa.NewClientCredentialsSource(xsuaa.Config{
    ClientID:     cb.ClientID,
    ClientSecret: cb.ClientSecret,
    TokenURL:     cb.TokenServiceURL + "/oauth/token",
})

dialer := connectivity.NewDialer(connectivity.Config{
    ProxyHost:   cb.OnpremiseProxyHost,
    ProxyPort:   cb.OnpremiseProxySocks5Port,
    TokenSource: connSrc,
})

conn, err := dialer.Dial(ctx, "internal-sftp.corp", 22, "")

The host and port must match a virtual mapping in Cloud Connector; the last argument is the Cloud Connector location ID (empty means the default location). You get back a plain net.Conn, so SSH, TLS or anything else can run on top.

Gotcha: when a dial fails, the error is a *connectivity.StageError that says whether it failed at dial, greeting, auth or connect. That tells you quickly whether to look at the token or at Cloud Connector access control.

For SFTP I also added sshclient.Dial, a thin wrapper that builds the SSH config from the destination and retries handshake failures with backoff.

3. From a Destination to a working HTTP client

Destination lookups use the same token pattern, built from the destination binding:

destSrc := xsuaa.NewClientCredentialsSource(xsuaa.Config{
    ClientID:     db.ClientID,
    ClientSecret: db.ClientSecret,
    TokenURL:     db.TokenServiceURL + "/oauth/token",
})
destClient := destination.NewClient(db.URI, destSrc, nil)

dest, err := destClient.Find(ctx, "MY_HTTP_DEST")

Then httpclient.New turns the destination into an *http.Client that applies its authentication and, for OnPremise destinations, routes through the Connectivity service's HTTP proxy:

cfg := httpclient.Config{}
if strings.EqualFold(dest.ProxyType, "OnPremise") {
    cfg.HTTPProxy = &httpclient.HTTPProxyConfig{Binding: cb}
}
client, baseURL, err := httpclient.New(dest, cfg)

resp, err := client.Get(baseURL + "/sap/opu/odata/sap/MY_SERVICE/Items?$top=5")

Gotcha: OData v2 writes need an X-CSRF-Token that is tied to a session cookie. The client keeps a cookie jar for that, and a helper fetches the token:

csrf, err := httpclient.FetchCSRF(ctx, client, baseURL+"/")
req.Header.Set("X-CSRF-Token", csrf) // then client.Do(req) for the POST

What it doesn't do

  • Client-credentials only. No principal propagation or user token exchange; everything runs as your service binding's technical client.
  • Secret-based bindings only. Bindings that use X.509 certificates instead of a client secret aren't handled.
  • sshclientskips SSH host-key checking by default. You can pass your own HostKeyCallback, and in anything beyond a demo you should.
  • Tested against fakes. The unit tests use local fake proxies and httptest servers, not a real Connectivity service, Destination service or Cloud Connector. [Author: state exactly what you have run end to end, e.g. whether you ran the Kyma path on a real cluster.]
  • Not an SAP product. It's an independent project, not provided or endorsed by SAP. It relies on service behaviour as I understood it from SAP's documentation and from observation, so check it against the current documentation for your landscape.

Quick start

The repository has three runnable Cloud Foundry examples (examples/sftp-count, examples/sftp-sshclient, examples/http-odata), each with a manifest and README. For the OData one:

cf create-service xsuaa application my-xsuaa
cf create-service connectivity lite my-connectivity
cf create-service destination lite my-destination

cd examples/http-odata
cf push
curl "https://<app-route>/odata?destination=MY_HTTP_DEST&path=/Items?%24top=5"

It needs Go 1.25 or later. Apart from sshclient, which uses golang.org/x/crypto, the packages use only the standard library, and there are no SAP-published Go dependencies. On my machine (Go 1.25.10, macOS arm64) go test -cover reports between about 70% and 94% statement coverage per module; that measures what the fakes exercise, not behaviour against real systems.

It's open source under the Apache License 2.0 at https://github.com/bluefunda/btp-go, with API docs at https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/bluefunda/btp-go. Several modules are still v0.x, so expect the API to change. Corrections are welcome, especially from anyone who has seen the Connectivity proxy behave differently in another landscape or on Kyma.

entry.title: Use SAP AI Core Models in VS Code Chat Without a Copilot Plan
entry.content:
VS Code’s Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) support lets developers use provider backed models in Chat without a Copilot plan. That can be useful when a team already has access to models through SAP AI Core and wants to work with them in VS Code.

There’s a small integration challenge with SAP AI Core service keys: they contain OAuth credentials and service URLs, not a standard model API key you can paste into a generic endpoint form. The client needs to exchange these credentials for an access token, then use that token and the correct resource group to make model requests.

I built SAPilot to handle those steps and make supported SAP AI Core deployments available in the VS Code Chat model picker.

What happens between Connect and Chat

After you enter your service key details, SAPilot stores the client secret in VS Code’s SecretStorage. The client ID, authentication URL, AI Core API URL, and resource group are stored separately as nonsecret connection settings. When SAPilot needs to call SAP AI Core, it requests an OAuth access token using the client credentials flow. The token is cached until shortly before it expires.

The exchange is the part that makes a service key different from a simple API key. This shortened example shows the same basic request SAPilot makes:

let tokenUrl = authUrl;
if (!tokenUrl.endsWith('/oauth/token')) tokenUrl += '/oauth/token';

const response = await fetch(`${tokenUrl}?grant_type=client_credentials`, {
  method: 'POST',
  redirect: 'error',
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Basic ${Buffer.from(`${clientId}:${clientSecret}`).toString('base64')}`
  }
});

if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`SAP sign-in failed: ${response.status}`);
const { access_token: accessToken, expires_in: expiresIn } = await response.json();

For a chat request, SAPilot sends the access token as a bearer token and adds the AI-Resource-Group header. It also discovers running deployments and chooses a compatible request format for each supported chat model. This is why connecting SAP AI Core takes more than entering a base URL and a key.

A small security decision with a practical effect

A design choice was where to persist the values entered during setup. SAPilot uses VS Code’s SecretStorage for the client secret and globalState for the client ID and endpoint details. VS Code documents SecretStorage as encrypted storage for sensitive values, while extension state is intended for ordinary key-value data. Keeping the secret out of ordinary configuration avoids writing it alongside nonsecret settings.

This choice also affects setup: the secret is stored locally through VS Code and is not synced between machines, so you enter it again on another machine. SAPilot never needs a shared credential embedded in the extension; each developer connects using their own service key. Prompts and chat context are sent to the SAP AI Core model selected in Chat, so the model and service key should be chosen according to your organization’s data and access policies.

Why use the Chat Provider API?

VS Code’s Language Model Chat Provider API lets an extension contribute models to the existing picker and handle requests for them. SAPilot registers a provider, looks up deployments available to the connected service key, and returns the supported chat deployments to VS Code. When you select one, the extension translates the chat messages into that model’s request format and streams the response back into Chat.

That provider layer is useful here because SAP AI Core can expose different model families and request formats. SAPilot currently handles supported OpenAI compatible Chat Completions, Claude, Bedrock Converse, Cohere Chat, and Gemini on Vertex AI deployments. Deployments that are not supported chat models, such as embeddings, are left out of the picker.

The result is a familiar workflow: connect once, open Chat, and select an SAP AI Core deployment. You do not need to copy an access token into VS Code or manually add a resource-group header for every request.

Getting started and scope

Install SAPilot in VS Code 1.104 or later, run SAPilot: Connect to SAP AI Core, and enter your service key details. You need permission to use a running chat deployment. Then open Chat and select a model under SAP AI Core.

BYOK makes this chat workflow available without a Copilot plan, but model usage still follows the billing terms of your SAP AI Core account. Some VS Code capabilities, including inline suggestions and semantic search, remain tied to GitHub or Copilot services. Model cost, quality, and speed depend on the deployment, usage, and task.

A takeaway and what’s next

SAPilot shows how VS Code’s BYOK support can connect developers to models their organization already provides through SAP AI Core. BYOK changes which service handles chat requests; model usage still follows your SAP AI Core billing and your organization’s data policies. If you try SAPilot, have a question, or would like to suggest a feature, let me know in the comments. You can also contribute by raising a pull request on GitHub.

References

  • Use your own language model key in VS Code
  • VS Code Language Model Chat Provider API
  • VS Code extension data storage and SecretStorage
  • SAP AI Core: Use a Service Key
  • SAPilot source code

entry.title: From Integration to Intelligence :Building enterprise-ready AI agents with Integration Suite & MCP
entry.content:
I have sat through a lot of agent demos this year. The pattern is usually the same. Someone types a request in plain English, the agent reads a purchase requisition, checks a budget, creates a purchase order in S/4HANA, emails the supplier, and posts a cheerful summary. The room claps. It is impressive.

Then I ask the question that integration people always ask: what happens on the 40,000th run? What happens when the supplier endpoint times out, when the mapping changes, when audit wants to know who approved what, or when the token bill arrives at the end of the month?

That is the gap between an agent that works in a demo and an agent that survives production. After close to two decades of building integrations, first on Oracle SOA and OSB, later on Boomi, Apigee and SAP BTP, my view is that the gap is mostly not a model problem. It is an architecture problem. And it is one the SAP integration community is unusually well placed to solve.

Last week I attended SAP's session "Building the Autonomous Enterprise with Integration Suite, AEM, and Agents" (13 October 2026). One line from it has stayed with me, because it captures the whole argument in eight words:

"Let the agent think. Let Integration Suite execute."

This post is my attempt to unpack that line from an architect's point of view: where agents earn their keep, where they should stay out of the way, and how API-centric integration and the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite connect the two.

1. The overloaded agent

When teams first build agents, they tend to give them everything. The agent calls the APIs, builds the payloads, decides on retries, transforms the formats and handles the errors. It feels efficient because there is only one component to think about.

It is not efficient. In effect you are asking a probabilistic reasoning engine to re-implement things your integration platform already does deterministically, with monitoring, retries and audit built in. Mapping JSON to IDoc, routing a message by company code, validating mandatory fields against a schema, sending a payment file over a bank channel: none of these need judgment. They need to be done exactly the same way every time.

The SAP session framed the consequences well, and they match what I have seen in practice:

  • Duplicated capability. The agent rebuilds APIs, EDI handling, mappings and routing you already own.
  • Reduced reliability. Predictable PO, invoice and payment flows start to depend on non-deterministic behavior.
  • Harder governance. Security, auditability and compliance become difficult to standardize when logic lives inside prompts.
  • Blurred accountability. When something fails, is it the reasoning, the integration, the partner or the backend? Nobody can tell quickly.
  • Higher operating cost. Tokens and agent capacity are spent on repetitive plumbing instead of the reasoning you actually wanted.

I like to describe it as driving a Lamborghini to the supermarket. You can, but it is not what the car is for, and the parking is a nightmare.

2. Who should own each step? A Procure-to-Pay test

The most useful part of the session, for me, was a simple step-by-step assessment of a standard Procure-to-Pay flow. For each step, it asked one question: is the value here in reasoning, or in reliable execution? I have adapted it below because I think every team should run this exercise on its own processes before writing a single prompt.

#

P2P step

Integration Suite value

Agent value

Owner

Why

1

Create requisition

Low

Medium

Agent

Demand signals need interpretation

2

Approve requisition

Low

High

Agent

Summarize context and policy, recommend

3

Create purchase order

Very high

Low

Integration Suite

Structured execution: APIs, EDI, mapping

4

Supplier acknowledgement

Very high

Low

Integration Suite

Receive, transform, update

5

Goods receipt

Very high

Very low

Integration Suite

Synchronization, not decisions

6

Very high

Low

Integration Suite

7

High

8

9

10

Low

Look at where the "Agent" rows sit. They are at the edges of the process: interpreting demand, explaining approvals, investigating exceptions and analyzing spend. The middle of the process, where money and goods actually move, belongs to integration. The three-way match is the interesting one. The match itself is a rule. The moment it fails, though, someone has to work out why, and that is exactly the kind of work an agent is good at.

So the question is not "agent or integration?" It is "which part of this step needs judgment?"

3. Two layers that work together

Once you accept that split, the architecture becomes cleaner. I think of it as two layers with a governed boundary between them.

The intelligence layer is where agents live, whether they are Joule agents, custom agents built on SAP BTP, or third-party agents. They understand the request, choose the right tools, interpret results, investigate exceptions and recommend or explain the next step.

The execution layer is SAP Integration Suite: Cloud Integration, API Management, Event Mesh, B2B and the connectivity into S/4HANA, ECC and third-party systems. It connects, transforms, routes, retries, secures and monitors.

An agent investigating a blocked invoice should never need to know how to reach the ERP, how to build the payload or which destination to use. It should ask for the evidence through an approved tool and spend its effort on explaining the discrepancy. The integration layer handles the rest.

Figure 1. Agents handle intent and reasoning; SAP Integration Suite provides governed access to business capabilities.

4. Why MCP matters here

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives compatible AI applications a standard way to discover and call tools. That sounds modest, but think about the alternative. Without a standard, every agent project discovers, interprets and rebuilds access to the same backends. The SAP deck compared it to a craftsperson. A good craftsperson is productive because trusted tools are already on the bench before the work starts. Agents need the same thing.

For a procurement agent, the bench might hold a handful of tools:

  • get_purchase_order to retrieve permitted PO details
  • check_approval_status to read the current approval state
  • validate_purchase_order to run defined validations
  • submit_for_approval to start an authorized approval workflow

Each tool has a clear purpose, a typed input and output contract, and narrow permissions. The agent picks the tool. The integration layer does the work.

One caution, because I hear this misunderstanding often: MCP standardizes the conversation between an agent and a tool. It does not make the tool secure, it does not check whether the user has authority to approve, and it does not guarantee the call succeeds. Those controls still live in the gateway, the integration logic and the backend.

5. Design tools for agents, not catalogs for agents

A typical SAP landscape has hundreds of APIs, iFlows and RFCs, many of them overlapping. The instinct is to expose all of them to the agent and let it figure things out. In my experience that is the fastest way to get an agent that is slow, expensive and unpredictable. Large tool catalogs make tool selection ambiguous, and oversized responses fill the context window with noise.

A lesson from one of my own programs: we built an AI assistant that answered purchase-order status questions for procurement and finance users, with a Vertex AI agent sitting behind Apigee X and calling into Ariba. Before it, these questions went into an email queue and often took a day to answer. After it, the answer came back in a few seconds. The model was not what made it work. What made it work was that the agent saw one narrow, well-described capability with a clean response, rather than the raw Ariba API surface. Most of the effort went into the API, not the prompt.

The same thinking applies to composition. Suppose an invoice-investigation agent needs invoice details, PO details and goods-receipt data. The naive design gives it three tools and asks it to correlate the responses. The better design composes them behind one business-oriented interface and returns a focused, structured result.

Figure 2. From multiple APIs to one agent-centric composed API.

This is now something SAP explicitly calls out: combining multiple backend APIs and exposing them as optimized MCP endpoints for agent consumption. The benefits are real (fewer tool calls, less correlation logic in the agent, smaller context, clearer ownership), but they are not free. Composition moves work into the integration layer, and its effect on latency and cost depends on data volumes, caching and how well you handle partial failures. Design it like any other API, with the same care.

The goal is not to expose more APIs to agents. It is to expose better business capabilities.

6. API-centric integration and the API artifact

Anyone who has worked on BTP for a while knows the split. Integration logic (routing, mapping, orchestration) lives in an iFlow in Cloud Integration. Exposure, security policies and throttling live in an API proxy in API Management. Two artifacts, two experiences, two places to look when something breaks.

API-centric integration introduces the API artifact, a single design and runtime element that combines the qualities of both: secure and publish, policy enforcement and throttling on one side; message routing, transformation and call orchestration on the other. It runs on the Integration Cell, a single runtime for Cloud Integration and API Management. According to the session, that removes extra hops and the double charging that came from passing a call through both. Monitoring is unified through the message processing log (MPL), with analytics feeding the existing API Management dashboards.

The capabilities that caught my attention as an architect:

  • Discovery of backend services from BTP destinations, the SAP Gateway catalog service for on-premise S/4HANA, and systems registered in the BTP cockpit's System Landscape.
  • API specifications attached as OpenAPI, or generated from natural language. A machine-readable spec is what lets an API be extended as an MCP tool, so this matters more than it looks.
  • Security with credentials scoped to a controlled set of APIs instead of master credentials, binding to XSUAA for token exchange across BTP, and principal propagation to on-premise systems. Validation of tokens from external OIDC issuers was shown as roadmap.
  • Developer Hub as one catalog where application developers subscribe to APIs and agents discover MCP servers, with self-registration for credentials.

On adoption, SAP's own recommendation was refreshingly conservative: consider the API artifact in the Integration Cell for greenfield projects, with no changes to existing deployments. I would put it this way:

  1. New work: design with the API artifact where the runtime and features you need are available.
  2. Stable integrations: leave them alone. A working iFlow that meets its SLA is not technical debt.
  3. Targeted modernization: consolidate when a flow is already being redesigned, or when a capability needs governed exposure to agents.
  4. Automation later: treat AI-assisted migration as something to evaluate once it is a supported capability, not something to plan budgets around today.

I have led enough migrations, from Oracle SOA 11g to 12c, from SOA to SAP BTP and from Boomi to Apigee X, to say this plainly: mass conversions without a business reason rarely pay back. Modernize where the change already touches.

7. Three paths to MCP with the MCP Gateway

This is the part I think matters most for SAP customers. The MCP Gateway in Integration Suite exposes your APIs, integrations and data sources as governed MCP servers. The session described three alternative starting points. They are options, not sequential steps.

Figure 3. Three paths to MCP enablement with SAP Integration Suite.

Path 1: from an API artifact. Expose a deployed API artifact's operations natively as MCP tools. This is the natural route for new API-centric work.

Path 2: from existing API specifications. Bring in specifications from existing API Management deployments or external HTTP endpoints. The technical spec is translated into MCP schema and enriched with natural-language semantics so agents can understand what each tool does.

Path 3: from RFCs. Expose remote-enabled function modules from ECC or S/4HANA. For a lot of customers this is the big one. Many core processes still run on ECC and on BAPIs that have been stable for fifteen years. Rebuilding every one of them as a new REST service before an agent can use it would delay adoption by years. That said, not every RFC should be agent-callable. Pick them deliberately, scope them tightly, and keep the backend authorization checks in place.

Two other points are worth noting. First, SAP Architecture Center now positions the MCP Gateway as the endorsed pathway for external third-party agents and for customer-built agents on BTP to reach SAP systems, with federation of third-party MCP servers on the roadmap. Second, MCP itself is still evolving quickly. If you run self-managed MCP servers, you own the job of tracking the specification and planning upgrades. A managed gateway takes that off your plate, which is a reasonable trade for most enterprise teams.

8. Guardrails are part of the design, not an add-on

In classic integration, it was usually enough to know that application X called API Y. With agents, you need to know which agent acted, on whose behalf, which tool it called, what authorization applied, and whether the business outcome was what everyone expected. Before any agent touches a transactional system, I want to see answers to these:

  • Identity and least privilege. Which agents and users can call which tools? Scoped credentials, not shared master keys.
  • Business authorization. Technical access must never bypass approval limits or segregation of duties. Being able to call submit_for_approval is not the same as being allowed to approve.
  • Input validation. Validate tool inputs against schema and business constraints before anything executes.
  • Traffic management. Rate limits, IP restrictions and payload protection, so a looping agent cannot flood an ECC system.
  • Error semantics. A rejected PO is a business outcome. An unreachable backend is a technical failure. The agent needs to be able to tell the difference.
  • Traceability. Enough logging to reconstruct a tool call end to end during an incident or an audit.
  • Human oversight. High-value or policy-sensitive actions go to a person. Design that path in from day one.

9. Context engineering is an integration concern

There is a common assumption that more context makes an agent smarter. Usually it does the opposite. Twenty overlapping tools and a 4,000-line payload make it harder for the model to choose correctly, and you pay for every token.

What works is focused tool descriptions, explicit input and output schemas, composed responses that contain only what the task needs, and retrieval on demand rather than up front. Notice that almost all of those are decisions made in the integration layer, not in the prompt. How well an agent behaves depends a great deal on what the surrounding architecture lets it see, reach and do.

10. Putting it together: invoice exception management

Here is how I would apply all of this to a scenario most SAP customers will recognize: thousands of supplier invoices a month, most of which match cleanly and a minority that do not.

Routine invoices never see an agent. Integration Suite ingests them, converts formats, runs the deterministic three-way match and posts them according to the rules. There is no reason to pay for reasoning on an invoice that matches.

Exceptions are where the agent comes in. When the match fails on a price variance, a missing goods receipt or a suspected duplicate, the agent calls a composed get_invoice_context tool, compares the evidence, explains the likely cause in plain language and recommends a next step.

Resolution stays controlled. The agent can trigger an authorized action within its limits or route a recommendation to an AP specialist. Either way, the integration layer validates the request and executes it with the normal controls.

Measurement decides whether it was worth it. I would track exception resolution time, the manual intervention rate, integration failure rate, cost per agent invocation and the share of cases resolved within policy. If those numbers do not move, the agent is a nice demo and nothing more.

11. A word on cost

Agent cost is not just tokens. It includes repeated tool calls, orchestration overhead, monitoring, governance and the time people spend investigating odd behavior. Keeping agents off deterministic steps is the single biggest lever. After that: reuse existing iFlows and APIs, keep responses small, compose where it saves calls, and measure consumption next to business outcomes. Edition requirements and AI-unit terms for these capabilities can change, so confirm current details with SAP before you build a business case.

Closing thoughts: orchestration, not universal agentization

The next phase of enterprise AI will not be won by the biggest model. It will be won by the teams that connect models to business processes without giving up the reliability, security and discipline that integration teams have spent years building.

If you are starting this week, here is what I would do:

  1. Take one end-to-end process, such as P2P, and score each step for reasoning value versus execution value.
  2. Pick one exception-heavy step where an agent clearly helps.
  3. Design two or three narrow, composed tools for it. Not twenty.
  4. Expose them through the MCP Gateway using whichever path fits: API artifact, existing spec or RFC.
  5. Put identity, authorization, rate limits and logging in place before go-live, and measure the outcome.

For those of us who have spent our careers in integration, this is good news. The skills that agentic AI needs most (clean contracts, governed access, reliable execution, good observability) are the ones we already have. Our job is not shrinking. It is moving one layer closer to the business.

I would like to hear how others are approaching this. Are you exposing RFCs to agents, or holding back until APIs are cleaner? Let me know in the comments.

entry.title: SAP BTP Hackathon 2026 最優秀賞個別インタビュー
entry.content:
はじめに 

本ブログは「SAP BTP Hackathon 2026」において、最優秀賞を受賞されたTISI株式会社様の個別インタビュー記事です。 

「SAP BTP Hackathon 2026」は、SAPジャパン株式会社の主催するパートナー/お客様向けのハッカソンイベントです。5年目の開催となった今年のハッカソンは、54社70チーム422名が参加されました。 

イベントの流れとしては、2026年5月よりイネーブルメントセッションを実施し、同年6月より1週間のハッカソンを行いました。その後SAPジャパンによる選考を経て、7/3(金)に一次選考を突破したファイナリストチーム6組が集まり、たくさんの参加者やSAP社員が見守る中で、渾身のプレゼンテーションを行い、最優秀作品とチームを決める最終選考イベントを実施いたしました。 

今年のハッカソンのテーマは、「業務プロセスを再設計せよ。〜 最強の“相棒”と創る、省力化と高度化のネクストステージ 〜」でした。このテーマにおいて、データに基づく継続的な監視と即時対応による意思決定の迅速化を目指し、社内ERPデータと外部市況情報を統合して経営指標の分析から将来シナリオ提示、アクション実行までを一気通貫で支援するアプリケーション「Joule自律的企業ナビゲーター～Joule Autonomous Enterprise Navigator～」を開発し、最優秀賞を受賞されたTISI株式会社（以下、TISI）“TISInnovators”チームの皆様に、お話をお伺いしました。

インタビュー内容 

Q1. 今回開発されたソリューションについて教えてください。具体的に誰のどのような課題を解決するものですか？ 

(藤本氏) 経営者や事業責任者が長年抱えてきた、「構造的な意思決定の限界」を打破するためのソリューションです。 

企業において、現場の情報は上位層に上がるにつれてどうしても解像度が落ち、タイムリーに届かず、多角的な判断を下すことも本質的に難しくなります。これはどれほど高額な業務システムを導入しても解決できなかった、人間の認知や組織構造に起因する限界と言えます。コンサルティングの現場でも、「情報の非対称性」や「判断の遅延」が経営の大きな足かせになっている場面を何度も目の当たりにしてきました。 

しかし、自律的に連携するAIエージェントの登場によって、「これなら長年の課題を解決できるのではないか」と思い立ち、その確信が出発点となりました。 

 

Q2. チーム編成の経緯や役割分担について教えてください。また、SAP BTPが初挑戦だったメンバーの学習面はいかがでしたか？ 

(有木氏) 上司から「メンバーを集めてみてほしい」と声をかけられた際、最初に考えたのは「勝てるチームの要件」でした。ハッカソンと聞くと技術者中心のイメージがあるかもしれませんが、実はそうではなく、ビジネス課題を定義できる人、それを技術で実現できる人、そして最後まで走り切れるモチベーションがある人。この三つが揃わないと戦えないと考えました。その3軸を念頭に置いて声をかけていきました。実務の都合で参加が難しいケースもありましたが、最終的に集まったメンバー間で話し合い、自然と役割分担ができていきました。 

SAP： AIエージェントなど、初めて触れる技術もあったと思いますが、キャッチアップはどのようにしましたか？ 

(馬場氏) 私は今回、Joule Studio（※2）を初めて扱いました。当初は不安もありましたが、ハッカソン向けに提供されたワークショップ資料が非常に体系的で、チュートリアルの完成度も高かったため、資料を起点にスムーズに理解を進められました。 

不明な点やつまずいた箇所があっても、実際に手を動かしながら試行錯誤を重ねることで、新技術の概念や具体的な実装方法についても短期間でしっかりとキャッチアップできました。未経験であることがハンデにならないよう、チーム全体でフォローし合える温かい雰囲気があったことも非常に大きかったです。 

SAP： キャッチアップや開発を進めるうえで、具体的に役立ったSAP公式のコンテンツやツールはありましたか？ 

(有木氏) いくつか非常に助けられたリソースがあります。 

まず、実装のキャッチアップで大いに活用したのがSAP Developer CenterのSAP Tutorials（※3）です。特にTutorial Navigatorのステップバイステップ手順は、BTPの最新技術の実装方法をキャッチアップするうえで欠かせないものでした。開発メンバーからも「チュートリアルが実装を進めるうえで役立った」との声が挙がっています。 

また、アーキテクチャ構成を検討するフェーズではSAP Architecture Center（※4）の構成図を参照しました。最新のソリューション構成が掲載されており、サービスの組み合わせや連携方法を理解するうえで有用でしたね。 

そして、ハッカソン全体を通して活用したのがSAP Joule for consultants（※5）です。 特に、要求仕様をSAP BTPの具体的な機能に落とし込む局面で重要な役割を果たしました。資料単体では腹落ちしきれない部分について SAP Joule for consultants に質問して解説してもらったり、実装中につまずいた箇所も頻繁に SAP Joule for consultants で確認しながら進めたりと、スペック作成から実装、レビュー、技術調査まで、幅広いシーンで利用しました。 

 

Q3. 最終案に至るまでに没になったアイデアはありましたか？また、アイデア選定の評価軸やチーム内での意見のすり合わせについて教えてください 

(有木氏) 最初はメンバーそれぞれが普段の業務で感じている課題をテーマに、アイデアを出し合いました。SAP導入プロジェクトのマネジメント支援や、システム運用保守における課題などです。ただ、「結局、誰の何の困りごとを解決したいのか？」という原点に立ち返った際、エンドユーザーに直接価値が届く「実業務」に近いテーマのほうが、訴求力も共感も高いという判断に至りました。 

(藤本氏) アイデアの選定では、各案をAIで解析し、5つの評価軸で採点した上で改善案を取り込むというサイクルを回しました。磨き込めばどの案もかなりの完成度まで持っていけます。だからこそ最後の決め手となったのは、「他と差別化できる圧倒的なインパクトがあるか」、そして「誰も解けていない本質的な問いを立てられているか」でした。 

SAP： チーム内で意見が対立するような場面はありましたか？ 

(有木氏) 衝突して意見がまとまらない、といった場面はほとんどありませんでしたね。声をかけたメンバーが、それぞれ現場で多様な経験を積んできたプロフェッショナルばかりだったので、自然と建設的な議論ができたのだと思います。 

(藤本氏) メンバーがシニア層中心で、現場の修羅場を経験してきた人たちだったため、対応が非常に大人でした。否定から入るのではなく、「その視点を活かすなら、こう発展させられるのではないか」という建設的な返しが自然にできていた。そこはチームの強みでした。 

(有木氏) 弊社はトップダウンというより、現場が主導して様々な検討を行い、形にしていくボトムアップの風土があります。今回のハッカソンも、まさにその風土が良い形で功を奏したのだと思います。方向性の異なる意見を柔軟に取り込むことで最終案がより磨かれていきました。たとえば、メンバーが出したアイデアを取り入れ、コンセプトを大きく洗練させていったプロセスがあるのですが、そのあたりの経緯は藤本から紹介してもらえますか。 

(藤本氏) もともとベースとしてあったのは、「AI社外取締役」というアイデアでした。経営会議の議題をAIが事前に整理し、複数のペルソナ（AI役員）が忖度なく意見をぶつけ合うという構想です。 

その複数ペルソナという軸をベースにしつつ、田畑の「AIエージェント全盛の時代だからこそ、人間が何をするかにフォーカスすべきだ」という重要な視点が加わりました。AIに判断を委ねるのではなく、人間中心の意思決定を支える存在としてペルソナ一人ひとりの人格や役割を再定義したことで、コンセプトが一気に洗練され、深みが増しました。 

SAP： 技術面の判断軸はいかがでしたか？ 

(森氏) SAPのビジョンであるAutonomous Enterpriseを先取りし体現するショーケースを目指し、「SAPのAI技術をどこまでフル活用できるか」を大きな判断軸としていました。SAP BTPという強力なプラットフォームがある以上、その可能性を最大限に引き出せる構成にしたいと考えたからです。 一方で、ハッカソンという限られた期間の中で実装まで到達し、審査員の方々に納得していただけるデモシナリオとして成立させることも重要です。最終的に採用したアイデアは、SAPのAI技術を幅広く網羅しながら、実装性とデモとしての分かりやすさのバランスを高いレベルで満たすものになりました。 

(馬場氏) SAP S/4HANA®（※6）との親和性も大きな判断軸でした。SAPの強みである企業の基幹業務データを最大限に活用できるソリューションであれば、実ビジネスにおけるリアリティが格段に増します。審査員にとっても「実際の現場で使えるイメージが湧くか」は極めて重要な評価ポイントになると考えており、その点において今回のソリューションが優れているという結論に至りました。 

(有木氏) 振り返ると、コンセプト・技術・ビジネス価値、それぞれの観点から各自の役割が自然に機能していました。もちろん現場プロジェクトではトップダウンの強いリーダーシップが求められる場面もありますし、そうした牽引が得意な人材もいます。状況に応じてアプローチを柔軟に使い分けられる点も、弊社の強みだと感じています。 

 

Q4. アーキテクチャや機能面を含め、開発を通じて最も効果的だった技術選択と、ハッカソン期間中に直面した壁をどう乗り越えたかを教えてください 

(森氏) 弊社ならではの工夫として、Joule（※7）とシングルページアプリケーション型のSAP Fiori®（※8）UIをシームレスに組み合わせた点があります。Jouleのチャット画面を入口としながら、必要に応じて分析結果や予測、対応策などの詳細画面へスムーズにドリルダウンできる構成にしました。チャットと画面の行き来が途切れないよう、UI5側の設計は中嶋が細部まで作り込んでくれました。 

また、9つのAIエージェントが司令塔となるオーケストレータを中心に連携し、情報収集から分析、予測、対応策の検討、最終的な人間の選択・承認、そしてその後のシステム実行まで、一連の業務プロセスをエンド・ツー・エンドの閉ループ（※9）で実現しています。単にAIエージェントを複数並べるのではなく、それぞれに明確な役割分担を持たせ、ひとつの業務プロセスとして高度にオーケストレーションした点が大きな特徴です。 

直面した壁は、当時の生成AIの応答特性を前提として、複数のAIエージェントが安定して連携する仕組みを構築することでした。そのため、システムプロンプトだけでなく、エージェント間の役割分担や情報の受け渡し方、検証プロセスなどを細かく設計し、品質向上を図りました。特にオーケストレーションにおいては、AIを単なるチャット相手ではなく、業務を正確に遂行する「ワーカー」として稼働させるため、期待する形式や内容を安定して出力させること、そしてその結果の正当性を検証することが不可欠になります。複数のエージェントをつなぐほど、1つの出力の揺らぎが後続処理全体に影響を及ぼすため、各エージェントの役割定義や入出力仕様を細部まで設計し、精度を高めていきました。 

(馬場氏) 技術的なコアは、メインのAIエージェントを司令塔に据えたマルチエージェントのオーケストレーション設計です。単一のAIにすべてを担わせるのではなく、業務フェーズごとに専門のサブエージェントを配置し、それぞれが「AIスキル」を通じてSAPシステムと安全に連携する構成としました。 AIスキルから呼び出されるSAP側のサービスは、板東がCAP・OData V4で実装しています。 メインのAIエージェントが全体のフローを統合し、人間との対話を一手に担うことで、「AIが人間の意思決定を黒子として支える」という理想的な協業モデルが具現化できたと考えています。 

 

Q5. 今回開発されたソリューションの現状の完成度と、今後のビジネス展開について教えてください 

(森氏) ソリューションの骨子は汎用性を持たせて設計しているため、業界や業種を問わず柔軟に応用できるアーキテクチャになっています。ただ、実際にお客様へ導入するにあたっては、個別のビジネスシナリオに合わせたチューニングが不可欠となるため、現状はPoC相当と位置づけています。まずは特定のお客様が抱える具体的な課題に深く刺さる成功実績を築き、そこから横展開を図っていくことが最も堅実なアプローチだと考えています。 

(藤本氏) 森の言う通りですが、PoCの初期ターゲットとしては、日本の大手製造業を強く意識しています。地政学リスクをはじめ、サプライチェーンのボラティリティが極めて高い業界であり、意思決定の迅速化に対するニーズが最も切実な領域だからです。コンサルティングの観点から見ても、「課題の深刻さ」と「解決できた際のインパクト」のバランスが最も優れており、ソリューションの価値を最大限に発揮できるターゲットだと確信しています。 

Q6. 見事グランプリを獲得されましたが、今回の勝利を象徴する最大の勝因は何だと考えていますか？ 

(藤本氏) 「ビジネスインパクトと革新性で圧倒的な結果を出す」という強いこだわりです。審査員の方々に価値が明確に伝わるものを作り上げることだけに集中しました。技術面は森をはじめとするエンジニア陣を全面的に信頼し、自身はビジネス価値の徹底的な訴求に徹しました。互いに信頼し合い、自然と役割分担が確立されていたこともチームとして大きかったですね。 

ファイナリスト選出後も、制限時間内に収めるためのトークスクリプトの推敲やデモ動画の再収録、投影時の視認性を考慮したプレゼン資料の見直しなど、細部まで徹底的にブラッシュアップしました。最後の最後まで妥協しなかった姿勢が、最高の結果につながったのだと思います。 

(森氏) 私は「このチームで優勝する」という明確なビジョンを描いており、そのための戦略として、SAPのAI技術の活用はもちろん、開発プロセスそのものにもAIをフル活用する方針を徹底しました。 

TISIではハッカソン以前からAIエージェント活用のR&Dを本格的に推進していたため、「この技術で何ができるのか」という解像度が他チームよりも格段に高かったと自負しています。その強みが顕著に表れたのが、お題発表の翌日にはすでに業務シナリオやユースケース、各ペルソナの期待役割などが詳細かつ明確に定義されていた点です。また、田畑と二人でSDD（仕様駆動開発）とTDD（テスト駆動開発）を組み合わせた開発手順を事前に整備していたことも大きかったですね。実装の道筋に迷う時間が一切なく、開発スピードを劇的に加速させることができました。 

実際の開発においてはClaude Code、Codexを活用し、ハーネスエンジニアリング（※10）の手法を適用することで、仕様に基づく実装からテスト、修正までの一連の工程をAIが反復的に実行できる体制を整えていました。 

(馬場氏) 開発が本格稼働した段階で、「少なくともファイナリストには残れるだろう」という確かな手応えがありました。「ここまで手を抜かずに作り込んで残れなければ仕方がない」と全員が胸を張れる水準までやり切ったことが、大きな勝因だったと感じています。 

(有木氏) 私個人としては、正直なところ優勝はおろかファイナリスト選出すら予想外でした（笑）。「何か新しい学びが得られれば」という自然体でスタートしたのですが、こうして振り返ると、メンバー全員がそれぞれの持ち場で、それぞれのやり方で確実に「勝ちに行っていた」のだと実感します。 

役割は異なっても、目指すベクトルは完全に一つでした。本質的な課題を発見し、チーム一丸となって最後まで形にし切る。それこそがTISIというチームの誇るべき「実現力」なのだと、改めて感じています。

今回の取材を通じて、ハッカソンにおけるSAP BTPや最新AI技術に対する参加者の熱気、そして実ビジネスへ適用する解像度の高さを肌で実感しました。今後、技術のさらなる進歩とともに、SAP BTPを活用したイノベーションがより一層盛り上がっていくことを確信しています。 

本記事が、SAP BTPやAI活用にこれから挑戦される皆さまや、まだ触れたことのない方々にとって、新たな一歩を踏み出すきっかけの一助となれば幸いです。（SAP 末次） 

 

注釈 

（※1）SAP Business Technology Platform（SAP BTP）：データ管理、アナリティクス、AI、アプリケーション開発、プロセスの自動化、統合機能をクラウド上で一元的に提供するSAPのビジネスプラットフォーム。2026年4月よりSAP Business AI Platformに名称変更。 

（※2）Joule Studio：SAPのAIソリューション「Joule」を拡張するだけでなく、AIエージェントやカスタムスキルの設計・構築・実行・管理を包括的に支援するSAPのAI開発ソリューション。ウェブUIとCLIに対応し、ローコード/ノーコードから本格的なコード開発まで幅広い開発スタイルをサポートする。 

（※3）SAP Tutorials：SAPの公式開発者ポータル「SAP Developer Center」内で提供されている学習コンテンツ群。SAPの最新技術や具体的な実装手順をステップバイステップで体験しながら学べる公式のハンズオンチュートリアル。 

（※4）SAP Architecture Center：SAPのベストプラクティスに基づいたリファレンスアーキテクチャやソリューション構成図、連携ガイダンスなどを提供するアーキテクト・開発者向けの公式ポータル。 

（※5）SAP Joule for consultants：SAP独自の包括的なナレッジベースやベストプラクティスに基づき、要件定義からソリューション設計、実装、技術調査までを支援するコンサルタント・エンジニア向けの会話型AIソリューション。 

（※6）SAP S/4HANA：企業の基幹業務をリアルタイムに統合管理する、SAPの次世代エンタープライズERPスイート。 

（※7）Joule：日常的な自然言語による指示から業務データの照会、インサイト抽出、プロセス実行までを支援するSAPの基幹AIコパイロット。 

（※8）SAP Fiori：直感的で統一感のある操作性を提供するSAPの標準デザインシステム、およびUIフレームワーク。 

（※9）閉ループ：情報の収集・分析から、予測、意思決定、そしてシステムへの実行までの一連の業務プロセスが、途中で分断されることなく一気通貫で完結・循環している状態のこと。 

（※10）ハーネスエンジニアリング：AIに白紙からコードを書かせるのではなく、仕様、テストケース、検証環境などの枠組みを人間があらかじめ設計・整備し、AIの生成精度と自律的な実装を担保する先端の開発手法。

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 4: Switching on Transport and the first transport
entry.content:
Part 4 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 3 we finished the receiving end in Central. All the pipes are in place. In this part we give the right person the right role, switch on Transport in Integration Suite, check every connection, and send the first package all the way to the target.

Step 1: Give yourself the transport role

Up to now every role went to a service instance. Clicking Transport is done by a person, so this one goes to a user.

  • In the Dev subaccount, go to Security > Role Collections and create a role collection, for example CPI-Transport.
  • Add the role WorkspacePackagesTransport and assign the collection to everyone who should be able to transport.
  • The same users also need the normal Integration Suite role collections (for example PI_Integration_Developer, and PI_Administrator for the settings in step 2).

After assigning roles, log out and in again or reload the browser tab. The old login does not know about the new role.

Step 2: Switch on Transport in Integration Suite

In the Dev Integration Suite, go to Settings > Integrations > Transport, choose Edit, set Transport Mode to Transport Management Service and save. Then choose Check Configuration. It tests the destinations from Part 2 and should end with success.

Step 3: Check the connection in Content Agent

Open the Content Agent UI (subscription) in Dev and go to Cloud Transport Management Service. With destination TransportManagementService selected, the status must say Connected, and you can pick the source node from Part 1. This is the check that catches wrong credentials, which Check Connection in the cockpit does not.

 

The same screen in my setup, before and after fixing the client ID.

Step 4: Send the first package

In Integration Suite, open a small test package under Design and choose Transport. Add a short comment and confirm. Integration Suite hands the package to Content Agent, Content Agent packs it, and the parcel lands at the source node and moves along the route to the target node.

Use a package with one simple iFlow for the first run. If something fails, you want the problem to be the setup, not the content.

Step 5: Import in CTMS

Open CTMS, go to the target node and open its import queue. Your transport request is waiting there. Select it and choose Import. CTMS hands the parcel to the second Content Agent through CAS_on_target, which writes the package into the target Integration Suite. When the status shows success, open the target workspace: the package is there.

The person who imports needs the CTMS role ImportOperator in a role collection (see the roles table in Part 1).

What tripped me up in my setup

  • Transport Mode stayed greyed out. I spent a long time on the wrong things: which runtime instance, which key, which destination. The real cause was simple: WorkspacePackagesTransport was not in the custom role collection I had assigned to my user in Dev. Once I added it, Transport Mode could be set. If this option is disabled for you, check the user's role collections first.
  • Integration Suite did not open properly in Dev. The Integrations area was not visible until I assigned the normal Integration Suite role collections (PI_Administrator, PI_Integration_Developer, PI_Business_Expert, PI_Read_Only) to my user. The transport role alone is not enough.
  • Check Configuration failed with a token error. My first check ended with "Failed to fetch auth token(Destination Name: ContentAssemblyService)". The useful part is the destination name at the end: it tells you exactly which of the three destinations cannot log in. Compare that destination's client ID, client secret and token URL (including /oauth/token) with its service key.
  • Content Agent said "Not Connected". The screenshot above is from my setup. The TransportManagementService destination looked fine in the cockpit, but its client ID did not match the CTMS key. After fixing it, the status changed to Connected.

What comes next

Integration packages now travel from Dev to Central. In Part 5 we use the same setup to transport something different: role collections.
